modules.title: 12.1 Air Pollution, Acid Rain and the Ozone Layer
modules.html:
Environmental chemistry studies the chemical species present in air, water and soil, how human activity changes them, and how the damage can be measured and reversed. Pollution is the introduction into the environment of a substance (a pollutant) in a concentration high enough to harm living things or property.

Composition of clean dry air

Gas% by volume
Nitrogen78.0
Oxygen21.0
Argon and other noble gases0.9
Carbon(IV) oxide0.03–0.04
Water vapour, dust, ozonevariable

Major air pollutants, sources and effects

  • Carbon(II) oxide, \(CO\): incomplete combustion in engines, generators and charcoal stoves. Forms carboxyhaemoglobin, starving tissues of oxygen; fatal in closed rooms.
  • Sulphur(IV) oxide, \(SO_2\): burning of sulphur-containing coal and oil and roasting of sulphide ores. Causes bronchitis and acid rain.
  • Oxides of nitrogen, \(NO_x\): formed in hot engines and by lightning. Cause acid rain and photochemical smog.
  • Hydrocarbons and particulates (soot): from vehicle exhausts, gas flaring and bush burning. Cause respiratory disease and cancer.
  • Lead compounds: formerly from leaded petrol; damage the nervous system, especially in children.
  • Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs): from old refrigerators and aerosols; destroy stratospheric ozone.

Acid rain

Normal rain is slightly acidic (pH about 5.6) because of dissolved \(CO_2\). Acid rain has pH below 5 and is caused by:

\(SO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_3\); \(2SO_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2SO_3\); \(SO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_4\); and \(3NO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow 2HNO_3 + NO\).

Effects: acidifies lakes and kills fish, leaches nutrients from soil, damages forests, corrodes metals and dissolves limestone and marble buildings. Control: flue-gas desulphurisation with limestone slurry, low-sulphur fuels, catalytic converters on vehicles, and liming of affected lakes and soils.

The ozone layer

Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation. Chlorine radicals released from CFCs by UV destroy it catalytically: \(Cl^{\bullet} + O_3 \rightarrow ClO^{\bullet} + O_2\), \(ClO^{\bullet} + O \rightarrow Cl^{\bullet} + O_2\); one chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. Thinning causes skin cancer, cataracts and reduced crop yields. The Montreal Protocol phased out CFCs in favour of HFCs and hydrocarbons.
examples: Write equations showing how SO2 in the air becomes sulphuric acid in rain.
Explain why one chlorine radical can destroy many ozone molecules.

modules.title: 12.2 Global Warming, Water and Soil Pollution
modules.html:
The greenhouse effect and global warming

Short-wavelength solar radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms the earth; the earth re-radiates longer-wavelength infrared. Greenhouse gases — \(CO_2\), \(CH_4\), \(N_2O\), CFCs and water vapour — absorb this infrared and re-emit it downwards, keeping the planet about \(33^{\circ}C\) warmer than it would otherwise be. The natural effect makes life possible; the enhanced effect from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and gas flaring causes global warming.

Consequences: melting polar ice and rising sea levels (a direct threat to Lagos, Port Harcourt and the Niger Delta), more intense flooding and drought, desertification in the far north, coral bleaching, shifting rainfall patterns and reduced crop yields.

Mitigation: renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro), afforestation, ending routine gas flaring, energy efficiency, carbon capture and storage, and cleaner cook-stoves.

Water pollution

  • Sewage and organic waste: raise the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD); bacteria decomposing the waste use up dissolved oxygen and fish suffocate. High BOD therefore means heavily polluted water.
  • Fertiliser run-off (nitrates and phosphates): cause eutrophication — algal bloom, blocked light, death and decay of algae, oxygen depletion and a dead water body.
  • Heavy metals (\(Pb^{2+}\), \(Hg^{2+}\), \(Cd^{2+}\)): from mining, batteries and industry; they are cumulative poisons that bioaccumulate up the food chain. Mercury poisoning (Minamata disease) damages the brain; lead causes anaemia and mental retardation; cadmium damages bones and kidneys.
  • Crude-oil spillage: a major Niger Delta problem; the oil film cuts off oxygen and light, kills fish and mangroves and destroys farmland and fishing livelihoods. Treatment uses booms, skimmers, dispersants and bioremediation with oil-degrading bacteria.
  • Thermal pollution: warm water from power stations lowers dissolved-oxygen solubility.

Water quality indicators

Dissolved oxygen (should exceed \(5\ mg\,dm^{-3}\) for fish), BOD (below \(3\ mg\,dm^{-3}\) is clean), pH (6.5–8.5), turbidity, total dissolved solids and coliform bacteria count. The World Health Organisation limit for lead in drinking water is \(0.01\ mg\,dm^{-3}\).

Soil and land pollution

Caused by indiscriminate dumping of refuse, plastics, agrochemicals, e-waste and industrial sludge. Persistent pesticides such as DDT are non-biodegradable and accumulate in food chains; excessive fertiliser acidifies soil and destroys structure. Remedies include controlled landfill, composting, crop rotation, organic manure, integrated pest management and remediation of contaminated sites.
examples: Explain the link between fertiliser run-off and fish deaths in a lake.
State three effects of crude-oil spillage on a Niger Delta community.

modules.title: 12.3 Waste Management, Sewage Treatment and Green Chemistry
modules.html:
Waste management: the waste hierarchy

  1. Reduce — use less material in the first place; refuse single-use plastics.
  2. Reuse — refill bottles, repair equipment.
  3. Recycle — reprocess paper, glass, aluminium and PET; recycling aluminium saves about 95% of the energy of primary extraction.
  4. Recover — compost organic waste; capture landfill methane or incinerate with energy recovery.
  5. Dispose — sanitary landfill with an impermeable liner and leachate collection, as the last resort.

Types of waste: biodegradable (food, paper, vegetation), non-biodegradable (plastics, glass, metals), hazardous (batteries, hospital waste, chemicals) and radioactive waste, which must be vitrified and stored in deep geological repositories.

Problems of open dumping and burning, still common in Nigerian cities: leachate contaminates groundwater, decaying refuse produces methane (explosive and a greenhouse gas), open burning of plastics releases dioxins and \(HCl\), and dumps breed rats, flies and mosquitoes that spread cholera and malaria.

Sewage treatment in outline

Primary: screening and sedimentation remove solids. Secondary: aerobic bacteria in trickling filters or activated-sludge tanks oxidise dissolved organic matter, drastically lowering BOD. Tertiary: removal of nitrates and phosphates, filtration and chlorination before discharge. Anaerobic digestion of the sludge yields biogas (about 60% methane) usable as fuel, and the digestate becomes fertiliser.

Green chemistry principles

  • Prevent waste rather than treat it afterwards.
  • Maximise atom economy: \(\text{atom economy} = \dfrac{\text{mass of desired product}}{\text{total mass of reactants}} \times 100\%\).
  • Use safer solvents (water, supercritical \(CO_2\)) and renewable feedstocks.
  • Use catalysts rather than stoichiometric reagents; design for degradation.

Nigerian and global policy

NESREA and the Federal Ministry of Environment enforce environmental standards; the Harmful Waste Act followed the 1988 Koko toxic-waste dumping incident. Internationally the Montreal Protocol (ozone), the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement (greenhouse gases) and the Basel Convention (transboundary hazardous waste) are the agreements most often named in examinations.
examples: List the five steps of the waste hierarchy in order of preference.
Describe the three stages of sewage treatment.

modules.title: 12.4 Environmental Calculations and Examination Technique
modules.html:
Environmental questions usually combine recall with a short calculation on concentration, atom economy or gas volume. These are the routines.

Parts per million

\(1\ ppm = 1\ mg\ per\ dm^3\ of\ water = 1\ mg\ per\ kg\).

Example: A water sample contains \(0.5\ mg\) of lead in \(2\ dm^3\). Express the concentration in ppm and state whether it meets the WHO limit of 0.01 ppm.

Concentration \(= 0.5/2 = 0.25\ mg\,dm^{-3} = \mathbf{0.25\ ppm}\), which is 25 times the WHO limit — the water is unsafe.

Mass of pollutant from combustion

Example: A fuel oil contains 2.0% sulphur by mass. What mass of \(SO_2\) is released when 1 tonne is burnt? (\(S=32, O=16\)).

Mass of sulphur \(= 0.02 \times 1000\ kg = 20\ kg\); \(n \propto 20/32\). Since \(S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2\) is 1:1, mass of \(SO_2 = 20 \times 64/32 = \mathbf{40\ kg}\).

Volume of a greenhouse gas

Example: What volume of \(CO_2\) at s.t.p. is produced by burning 1.6 kg of methane completely? (\(C=12, H=1\)).

\(CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O\). \(n(CH_4) = 1600/16 = 100\ mol\), so \(n(CO_2)=100\ mol\) and \(V = 100 \times 22.4 = \mathbf{2240\ dm^3}\).

Atom economy

Example: In \(CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\), the desired product is quicklime. Atom economy \(= 56/100 \times 100 = \mathbf{56\%}\). The remaining 44% leaves as \(CO_2\), which is why cement manufacture is a large carbon emitter.

How to write a good essay answer

Name the pollutant, give its source, write a chemical equation where one exists, describe the effect on health or the environment, and finish with a named control measure. Four clear points score far better than a page of generalities such as "pollution is bad".
examples: Calculate the ppm of a solution containing 4 mg of nitrate in 5 dm3 of water.
Find the atom economy for producing iron from Fe2O3 by reduction with CO.

quiz.solution: They oxidise CO and hydrocarbons and reduce NOx.

quiz.solution: Much oxygen is being consumed by decomposition.

quiz.solution: Nutrients trigger algal blooms that later deplete oxygen.

fish death, algal bloom, oxygen rise

quiz.solution: Itai-itai disease is caused by cadmium.

quiz.solution: Concentrations rise at each trophic level.

quiz.solution: Gas solubility decreases as temperature rises.

quiz.solution: Plastics resist microbial breakdown.
